units.title: C++ basics
units.summary: The parts of a C++ program, output with cout, variables and data types, assignment, scope, arithmetic, comments and named constants.

lessons.title: Program parts, cout and #include
lessons.html:
A C++ program is built from a few standard pieces. Lines beginning with # are preprocessor directives, carried out by the preprocessor before the compiler runs; #include <iostream> pastes in the header file that declares cout and cin. using namespace std; lets you write cout instead of std::cout. Every program has exactly one function named main; execution always begins in main. Braces { } enclose the body, and return 0; reports success to the operating system.

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int main()
{
    cout << "Hello" << endl;
    return 0;
}

Each statement ends in a semicolon. Directives (#include) are not statements and take no semicolon. Whitespace and line breaks between tokens are ignored, so one statement may span several lines. Key words (int, return, const) are reserved; programmer-defined names are ones you invent; literals (5, "Hi") are values typed directly in the code; operators (<<, +) do work; punctuation (;, {, ,) separates things.

The cout object

cout is the standard output stream object. << is the stream insertion operator: it sends the value on its right into the stream on its left. Insertions chain left to right: cout << "x = " << x << endl;. Output is exactly what you insert; nothing adds spaces or line breaks for you. A string literal goes between double quotes and cannot span source lines.

endl ends the line and flushes the output buffer. The escape sequence \n inside a string only ends the line. An escape sequence is typed as a backslash plus a character but is stored as one character, so "a\tb" holds 3 characters:

SequenceMeaning
\nnewline
\thorizontal tab
\\one backslash
\"a double quote
\'a single quote
\aalert (bell)
\rcarriage return

10th edition addition: a raw string literal is written R"(text)". Everything between ( and ) is taken literally, backslashes included, and it may span several lines. R"(C:\temp\new)" prints C:\temp\new with no tab or newline. Trap: forgetting a semicolon, writing cout >> x, or leaving out #include <iostream> all fail to compile. Writing /n with a forward slash is not an escape sequence: cout prints a slash and an n.

More terms and rules

  • A header file holds declarations the compiler needs for library features; #include inserts it. A stream is a flow of characters: cout is the output stream, cin the input stream, and >> (the stream extraction operator) pulls data out of cin.
  • Arithmetic operators bind tighter than <<, so an expression inside a chain is worked out first and its result is inserted. A quoted digit is text, not a number:
cout << 4 + 1 << "x" << 2 * 3;   // 5x6

lessons.title: Variables, literals, assignment and identifiers
lessons.html:
A variable is a named location in memory that holds a value of one data type. It must be defined before use: int count; gives it a name, a type and storage. A value is placed in it by an assignment statement: count = 12;. The = operator copies the value of the right side into the variable on the left, so the left side must be a variable; 12 = count; is an error. Assignment is not an equation: x = x + 1; is legal and adds one.

int a = 5;
int b = a;   // copy: b is 5
a = 9;       // b is still 5

A literal is a value written directly in code: 42 (integer), 3.5 (floating point), 'z' (character), "zebra" (string). A name that stands for a value is not a literal.

Identifiers

An identifier is a name the programmer chooses. Rules: letters, digits and underscore only; it must not start with a digit; no spaces or punctuation such as -, $, .; it cannot be a reserved key word; and it is case sensitive, so Sales, sales and SALES are three different names.

NameLegal?Why
total_2yes
_holdyesunderscore may lead
2ndnostarts with a digit
my totalnocontains a space
net-paynohyphen is the minus operator
doublenokey word
Countyesdiffers from count

Good names describe their purpose (monthlyPay, not x), which makes the program self-documenting. Common styles are camelCase and snake_case; pick one and keep it. Exam traps: an identifier that is legal but misspelled differently on a later line is a different, undefined variable; and a variable defined twice in the same scope is an error.

More terms

  • Literals are also called constants in the book's older wording, because their value never changes.
  • The left side of = must be an lvalue: something that names a memory location whose contents can change, normally a variable. The right side can be any rvalue, meaning any expression that has a value (a literal, a variable's value, a calculation).
  • A variable that is defined but not given a value holds an unknown leftover value until you store something in it.

lessons.title: Integer types and char
lessons.html:
Integer types hold whole numbers. In increasing size: short, int, long, long long. The standard guarantees only the ordering short <= int <= long <= long long; exact byte counts depend on the system (commonly 2, 4, 4 or 8, 8). unsigned before a type uses the same storage for non-negative values only, which roughly doubles the largest positive value it can hold. Each type has a minimum and maximum; going outside it is overflow (Chapter 3).

Integer literals

  • 25 is decimal; a leading 0 makes octal, so 012 is 10; 0x1F is hexadecimal (31).
  • 10th edition: 0b1010 is a binary literal (value 10).
  • 10th edition: a single quote may separate digits for readability: 1'000'000 equals 1000000. The separators do not change the value.
  • Suffixes on whole numbers: L long (32L), LL long long, U unsigned. unsigned alone means unsigned int.

The char type

char holds one character, stored as a small integer code (ASCII on most systems; 'A' is 65, 'a' is 97, '0' is 48). A character literal uses single quotes: 'A'. A string literal uses double quotes: "A". They are different: "A" is two bytes, the letter plus a hidden null terminator (\0, code 0) that C++ stores at the end of every string literal, so "Dayton" occupies 7 bytes. A string literal cannot be stored in a char: char c = "Z"; does not compile.

char c = 'a';
c = c + 2;            // c is now 'c'
cout << c << endl;    // prints c

Because char is a number, you can do arithmetic on it. cout prints a char as a character but an int as a number. Trap: 'ab' is not a valid char literal (a char holds one character), and '\n' is one character even though it is written with two symbols.

Extra rules

  • sizeof(x) is an operator that returns how many bytes a type or variable takes; the ordering guarantee is sizeof(short) <= sizeof(int) <= sizeof(long).
  • A char may be given a character literal or a small whole number (its code): char grade = 66; stores the code for 'B' and prints B.
  • Suffix summary: on a number without a decimal point, L is long, LL long long, U unsigned. On a number with a decimal point, the suffix F makes a float and L a long double, and no suffix means double. So 500L is a long integer but 500.0L is a long double.

lessons.title: string, floating point, bool and sizeof
lessons.html:
The string class needs #include <string>. A string object holds text of any length: string city = "Dayton";. Useful members: city.length() (6), city[0] ('D', indexes start at 0), and + to concatenate: city + ", OH". Trap: you cannot add two string literals ("a" + "b" fails); at least one side must be a string object.

Floating point

float, double and long double store numbers with fractional parts, in increasing precision and range. double is the default for literals like 3.14; 3.14f (or F) is a float and 3.14L a long double. There are no unsigned floating-point types. E notation writes a power of ten: 3.2E4 is 32000 and 2.5e-2 is 0.025. The part before the E is the mantissa; the part after is the power of 10. To convert, move the point until one digit is left of it: 0.0072 is 7.2E-3. By default cout shows at most 6 significant digits and drops trailing zeros, so 5.0 prints 5.

bool

bool holds true or false; an expression whose value is true or false is a Boolean expression. Internally true is 1 and false is 0, and cout prints them as 1 and 0. Any non-zero value stored in a bool becomes true: bool f = 5; stores 1.

sizeof

sizeof is an operator giving the number of bytes a type or variable occupies, for example sizeof(int). Sizes vary between systems, so never assume a fixed answer. Only the ordering rules above are guaranteed.

TypeHolds
intwhole number
doublefractional number, about 15 digits
charone character
stringtext (library class)
booltrue or false

More string and Boolean facts

  • s += "text"; appends to the string s. length() counts characters stored, not the hidden terminator, and an escape sequence counts as one: string s = "ab\tc"; has length 4.
  • Boolean expression is the name for an expression that is true or false (after the logician George Boole).

lessons.title: Initialization, scope and arithmetic
lessons.html:
You can initialize a variable when defining it: int n = 4;, int n(4); or, in C++11 and later, brace initialization int n{4};. Brace initialization rejects narrowing: int n{9.99}; is an error, whereas int n = 9.99; compiles and stores 9 (the fraction is truncated, not rounded). auto lets the compiler deduce the type from the initializer: auto r = 5.0 / 2; makes r a double. A value assigned in a chain, a = b = 7;, is evaluated right to left. In int w = 8, h, d = 3; only w and d are initialized: each initializer belongs to one name. The left operand of = must be an lvalue (it names a memory location that can change, usually a variable); the right side is an rvalue, any expression that has a value.

Scope

A variable's scope is the part of the program where its name is visible: from its definition to the closing brace of the block that holds it. Using a variable on a line before its definition is a compile error, because the compiler reads top to bottom. A variable defined in main cannot be seen in another function. An inner block may define a name that shadows an outer one; the inner one wins inside its braces.

int x = 1;
{
    int x = 2;
    cout << x << " ";   // 2
}
cout << x;              // 1

Arithmetic

The values an operator works on are its operands. A unary operator takes one (negation, -x), a binary operator two (+, =), and C++ has one ternary operator, taking three (Chapter 4).

OperatorMeaning
+ - *add, subtract, multiply
/divide
%remainder (integers only)
  • If both operands are integers, / discards the fraction: 17 / 5 is 3, and 7 / 2 is 3 even when stored in a double. Make one operand floating point (7 / 2.0) to get 3.5.
  • 17 % 5 is 2. % does not compile with a double operand. n % 10 is the rightmost digit of n and n / 10 drops it. % never means percent: 15 percent of price is price * 0.15.
  • Precedence: * / % before + -; equal precedence goes left to right. 2 + 3 * 4 - 8 / 2 % 3 is 2 + 12 - 1 = 13.
  • Parentheses override precedence.

The traps are always the same: integer division inside a double assignment, and forgetting that % and / share a level with *.

Terms to know

TermMeaning
initializationgiving a variable its first value in its own definition (double rate = 0.05;); a later rate = 0.06; is an assignment
uninitializeddefined with no value (like h above): contents unknown
moduluscommon name for %, the remainder operator
unary / binary / ternaryone / two / three operands; -x is unary, a - b binary
lvalue / rvalueassignable location / any expression with a value
scopewhere a name is visible

The parentheses form also truncates: int n(9.99); stores 9.

lessons.title: Comments, named constants and style
lessons.html:
Comments are ignored by the compiler and explain the code to people. // text runs to the end of the line. /* text */ can span many lines and cannot be nested. Reversing the symbols (*/ ... /*) or forgetting the closing */ stops the program from compiling. Put a header comment at the top of each program (purpose, author, date) and brief notes before tricky steps. A comment that merely repeats the code adds nothing.

// computes pay for one week
/* the next line is disabled
   cout << "debug";
*/

A named constant is a variable that cannot change after it is set. Define it with const and you must initialize it in the same statement: const double TAX_RATE = 0.07;. Assigning to it later is a compile error, and const int LIMIT; with no value is also an error. By convention (not a rule) the names are written in capitals.

A raw number in the middle of a calculation is a magic number: its meaning is not obvious and changing it means hunting through the program. A named constant documents the meaning and lets you change it in one place.

Programming style is how code is laid out: consistent indentation (each nested block indented a few spaces), braces lined up, one statement per line, blank lines between logical sections, and meaningful names. Style never changes how the program runs, since the compiler ignores whitespace, but it decides whether other people (and you in a month) can read it.

constexpr is a stricter alternative to const: it requires a value the compiler can work out at compile time, and also makes the name read-only (constexpr double RATE = 0.07;).

questions.prompt: Which line of a C++ program is a preprocessor directive?
questions.explain: Preprocessor directives begin with # and are handled before compilation. The other lines are a using directive, a function header and a statement.

questions.prompt: In the statement cout << x;, what is the name of the << operator?
questions.explain: << inserts data into the output stream. The extraction operator >> is the one used with cin.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume the usual #include lines and using namespace std;.)
questions.explain: \n inside the string and endl both end a line. C and D are printed with nothing between them.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume the usual #include lines and using namespace std;.)
questions.explain: \" prints a double quote and \\ prints a single backslash.

questions.prompt: Both endl and the \n escape sequence move the cursor to the next line, but endl also flushes the output buffer.
questions.explain: That is the difference. \n only inserts a newline character; endl inserts it and forces buffered output out.

questions.prompt: Every complete C++ statement ends with which punctuation character? (Name it or type it.)
questions.explain: The semicolon terminates a statement. Preprocessor directives and function headers do not take one.

questions.prompt: Which statement displays Hi and then moves to a new line?
questions.explain: The correct form uses << and a quoted literal and ends with a semicolon. The others use the wrong operator, treat Hi as an undeclared variable, or omit the semicolon.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Raw string literals are a 10th edition feature. (Assume the usual includes and using namespace std;.)
questions.code:
cout << R"(C:\temp\new)" << endl;
cout << R"(He said "no")" << endl;
questions.explain: In a raw string literal R"(...)" backslashes are ordinary characters and quotes need no escaping, so the text is printed exactly as written.

questions.prompt: In the raw string literal R"(a\nb)", the \n is treated as a newline character.
questions.explain: Raw strings do not process escape sequences. The backslash and the n are two ordinary characters, so a\nb is printed literally.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume the usual #include lines and using namespace std;.)
questions.explain: The expressions are evaluated first: 2 + 3 is 5, the literal "5" is text, 2 * 3 is 6. No spaces are inserted, so the output runs together as 556.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a legal C++ variable name?
questions.explain: Names may begin with a letter or underscore but not a digit, and may not contain spaces or hyphens.

questions.prompt: Which of these cannot be used as a variable name?
questions.explain: int is a reserved key word. Total, total_1 and _x are all legal.

questions.prompt: In C++, the names Sales and sales refer to two different variables.
questions.explain: Identifiers are case sensitive, so differing capitalization makes different names.

questions.prompt: What is the term for a value typed directly into a program, such as 42 or "hello"?
questions.explain: A literal is a value written in the source code itself, as opposed to a name that stands for a value. The textbook notes that literals are also called constants.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume the usual #include lines and using namespace std;.)
questions.explain: y received a copy of x's value when it was initialized, so changing x later does not affect y.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume the usual #include lines and using namespace std;.)
questions.explain: After a = b, a is 10. Then b becomes the new a plus 1, which is 11.

questions.prompt: Which assignment statement will NOT compile?
questions.explain: The left operand of = must be an lvalue: something, usually a variable, that names a memory location whose contents can change. A literal such as 5 cannot be assigned to. The other three are legal; a = a + 1 adds one to a.

questions.prompt: A C++ variable name is allowed to begin with an underscore.
questions.explain: Identifiers may start with a letter or underscore. They may not start with a digit.

questions.prompt: Which statement about integer type sizes does the C++ standard guarantee?
choices: An int is always exactly 4 bytes
A long is always exactly 8 bytes
A short is always exactly 2 bytes
questions.explain: Only the ordering is guaranteed. Exact sizes depend on the compiler and system.

questions.prompt: An unsigned int variable can store negative numbers as long as they are small.
questions.explain: unsigned means the type holds only zero and positive values; the freed sign bit gives a larger positive range instead.

questions.prompt: Which data type holds exactly one character?
questions.explain: char stores a single character as a small integer code.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Assume the ASCII character set. (Assume the usual #include lines and using namespace std;.)
questions.explain: A char is a small integer, so adding 2 to the ASCII code for a (97) gives 99, the code for c. cout prints a char variable as a character.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between 'A' and "A" in C++?
choices: 'A' is a string literal and "A" is a char literal
Single quotes are for numbers and double quotes are for letters
'A' is a char literal; "A" is a string literal that also holds a null terminator
questions.explain: Single quotes make one char; double quotes make a string literal (a character array including the invisible null terminator).

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume the usual #include lines and using namespace std;.)
questions.explain: 0b1010 is binary for 10. The digit separator in 1'000 is ignored, so b is 1000 and b + 1 is 1001. (Binary literals and digit separators are C++14/10th edition features.)

questions.prompt: The literals 1'000'000 and 1000000 have the same value.
questions.explain: A digit separator is only for readability and does not change the value.

questions.prompt: What value is stored by int x = 012; ?
choices: The line is a compile error
questions.explain: A leading 0 makes the literal octal. Octal 12 is 1*8 + 2 = 10.

questions.prompt: What does placing the word unsigned before an integer type do?
choices: It doubles the number of bytes used
Same storage size, no negative values, and a larger maximum positive value
questions.explain: unsigned reuses the sign bit as part of the magnitude, so the range runs from 0 up to roughly twice the signed maximum.

questions.prompt: Which header must be included to use the string class?
questions.explain: The string class lives in <string>. <cstring> is the old C-style string library, a different thing.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume the usual #include lines and using namespace std;.)
questions.explain: + concatenates strings to give network, which has 7 characters.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume the usual #include lines and using namespace std;.)
questions.explain: 1.5e3 means 1.5 times 10 to the 3, which is 1500. 2.5E-2 is 0.025. cout drops unneeded trailing zeros.

questions.prompt: Which statement fails to compile?
questions.explain: Two string literals are not string objects, so + cannot join them. In every other choice at least one operand is a string object.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume the usual #include lines and using namespace std;.)
questions.explain: Any non-zero value becomes true (printed as 1) and zero becomes false (printed as 0).

questions.prompt: A float has more precision than a double.
questions.explain: double is the larger type and carries more significant digits than float.

questions.prompt: Which operator reports how many bytes a type or variable occupies?
questions.explain: sizeof gives a size in bytes; its exact values depend on the system.

questions.prompt: Which literal has type double?
questions.explain: A number with a decimal point and no suffix is a double. 3 is an int, 3.0f is a float, and '3' is a char.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume the usual #include lines and using namespace std;.)
questions.explain: Integer division gives the quotient 3 and % gives the remainder 2.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume the usual #include lines and using namespace std;.)
questions.explain: Both operands are integers, so 7 / 2 is already 3 before it is stored. Storing it in a double does not bring the fraction back.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume the usual #include lines and using namespace std;.)
questions.explain: One operand is a double, so the division is done in floating point and gives 3.5.

questions.prompt: What is stored by int n = 9.99; ?
questions.explain: Assigning a double to an int truncates the fraction. It does not round.

questions.prompt: What type does the compiler give x in auto x = 5.0 / 2; ?
questions.explain: 5.0 is a double literal, so the quotient is a double, and auto deduces double.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume the usual #include lines and using namespace std;.)
questions.explain: The inner x shadows the outer one inside the braces and ceases to exist at the closing brace. The outer x is still 1.

questions.prompt: Which expression does NOT compile?
questions.explain: The % operator accepts only integer operands.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume the usual #include lines and using namespace std;.)
questions.explain: * / % share one level and go left to right: 8 / 2 is 4, then 4 % 3 is 1. The result is 2 + 12 - 1.

questions.prompt: The statement int n{9.99}; compiles and stores 9.
questions.explain: Brace initialization forbids narrowing conversions such as double to int, so the standard makes this an error. The = and () forms (int n = 9.99; or int n(9.99);) quietly truncate to 9.

questions.prompt: Which arithmetic operator gives the remainder of an integer division?
questions.explain: The % operator, often called modulus, returns the remainder.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a legal multi-line comment?
questions.explain: /* begins the comment and */ ends it, and it may span lines. // comments only last to the end of one line.

questions.prompt: Which constant definition is invalid?
questions.explain: A const must be given its value in its definition, since it cannot be assigned to afterwards.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume the usual #include lines and using namespace std;.)
questions.explain: The comments are ignored, and the disabled statement never runs. 3 * 7 is 21.

questions.prompt: Which key word makes a variable a named constant that cannot be changed after initialization?
questions.explain: const (or constexpr for compile-time constants) marks a variable read-only.

questions.prompt: What is a magic number?
choices: A number that is always prime
An unexplained literal value in the code whose meaning is not obvious
questions.explain: Replacing magic numbers with named constants documents their meaning and lets you change them in one place.

questions.prompt: In the expression -total, the minus sign works on a single operand. What kind of operator is it?
questions.explain: Operators are named by how many operands they take: unary one, binary two, ternary three. Used for negation, - is unary; in a - b it is the binary subtraction operator.

questions.prompt: The assignment operator = is a binary operator.
questions.explain: It has two operands: the variable on its left and the value on its right. Unary operators take one operand, and C++ has a single ternary operator, which takes three.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume the usual #include lines and using namespace std;.)
questions.explain: The newline escape sequence is a backslash followed by n. /n uses a forward slash, so it is not an escape sequence and cout prints the slash and the n as ordinary characters. Only the final \n ends the line.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume the usual #include lines and using namespace std;.)
questions.explain: Each escape sequence is stored as one character even though it is typed with two symbols. The string holds a, b, a tab, c and a newline: 5 characters.

questions.prompt: How many bytes of memory does the string literal "Dayton" occupy? (A char uses 1 byte.)
questions.explain: The six letters are followed by the null terminator (\0) that C++ stores at the end of every string literal, so the literal takes 7 bytes. (A string object holding Dayton still reports length() as 6; the terminator is not counted.)

questions.prompt: Which definition does NOT compile?
questions.explain: "B" in double quotes is a string literal (a B plus a null terminator), and a string cannot be stored in a char. A char takes a character literal in single quotes or a small integer code such as 66.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Assume the ASCII character set. (Assume the usual #include lines and using namespace std;.)
questions.explain: A char stores a numeric code, and cout prints a char variable as the character with that code. In ASCII, 72 is H and 73 is I.

questions.prompt: Which is the E notation form of 0.000418?
questions.explain: Moving the decimal point 4 places to the right gives 4.18, so the power of ten is -4. 4.18E4 is 41800, and both 4.18E-3 and 41.8E-4 equal 0.00418.

questions.prompt: In the E notation value 6.25E8, the part before the E (6.25) is called the ____.
questions.explain: The mantissa is multiplied by the power of ten written after the E, so 6.25E8 means 6.25 times 10 to the 8th, or 625,000,000.

questions.prompt: C++ provides unsigned versions of float and double for values that are never negative.
questions.explain: There are no unsigned floating-point types. float, double and long double always hold both positive and negative values; unsigned applies only to the integer types.

questions.prompt: Which literal is a long integer literal?
questions.explain: The L suffix on a whole number makes it a long. LL makes a long long integer literal, and on a number with a decimal point L means long double and F means float.

questions.prompt: Why is `12 = count;` rejected by the compiler? The left side of an assignment must be what kind of operand, one that names a changeable memory location?
questions.explain: An lvalue can appear on the left of an assignment. The right side only needs an rvalue, any expression that has a value. That is why 12 = count; is an error.

questions.prompt: Giving a variable its first value as part of its definition, as in double rate = 0.05;, is called ____.
questions.explain: Initialization happens in the definition itself. A later statement such as rate = 0.06; is an assignment, not an initialization.

questions.prompt: After this definition, which variables have been given a value?
choices: none; the line does not compile
questions.explain: Each initializer belongs only to the name just before it. height is defined but left uninitialized, so its contents are unknown until something is stored in it.

questions.prompt: Why does this program fail to compile?
choices: cost is used before it is defined
a variable definition must also give the variable a value
questions.explain: A variable's scope begins at its definition and the compiler reads top to bottom, so the assignment on the line above the definition refers to an unknown name. Move double cost; above it, or write double cost = 19.95;.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume the usual #include lines and using namespace std;.)
questions.explain: n % 10 is the rightmost digit, 9. n / 10 is 472 (integer division drops the last digit), and 472 % 10 is 2. n / 1000 keeps only the thousands digit, 4.

questions.prompt: price is a double. Which expression computes 15 percent of price?
questions.explain: In C++ % is the modulus operator, never percent, and it does not accept a double operand. Write a percentage as a decimal: 15 percent is 0.15.

questions.prompt: When are preprocessor directives such as #include carried out?
choices: After compilation, while the program is being linked
Before the compiler translates the program
questions.explain: The preprocessor reads the source first and carries out the lines that begin with #, for example inserting the contents of iostream. The compiler then works on the result.

questions.prompt: Every C++ program must contain a function named main.
questions.explain: main is the starting point of every C++ program. A program may have many functions, but without main it cannot be built into a runnable program.

questions.prompt: Why does this program fail to compile?
choices: The comment symbols are reversed: a multi-line comment must start with /* and end with */
A multi-line comment must span at least two lines
The expression 0.18 * 50 must be in parentheses inside cout
questions.explain: */ only ends a comment; it cannot start one. Here */ is read as code, and the /* at the end of the first line opens a comment that is never closed, swallowing the rest of the file.

questions.prompt: A program typed with several statements on one line and no indentation will not compile.
questions.explain: The compiler ignores spacing and line breaks between the parts of a statement, so badly laid-out code still compiles. Programming style matters because people have to read the code.

questions.prompt: The name of a constant defined with const must be written in all uppercase letters, or the program will not compile.
questions.explain: Uppercase names such as TAX_RATE are only a convention that makes constants easy to spot. The compiler requires the const qualifier and an initial value, not capital letters.

questions.prompt: Which line correctly includes the iostream header file?
questions.explain: A directive begins with #, and the name of a standard header file goes inside angle brackets. Directives are not statements, so no semicolon follows.

questions.prompt: Using descriptive names such as hoursWorked instead of x helps make a program ____, meaning a reader can understand it largely from the code itself.
questions.explain: A self-documenting program explains itself through well-chosen names. Named constants such as TAX_RATE do the same for fixed values.

lessons.title: cin and mathematical expressions
lessons.html:
The idea: your program asks, the user types, cin delivers

Until now every program has only printed. To make it interactive it must also read what the user types. C++ does that with cin (say "see-in"), the standard input object. It comes from <iostream>, the same header as cout.

int age;
cin >> age;     // wait for the user to type a number, store it in age

>> is the stream extraction operator. It extracts (pulls out) a value from the input and stores it in the variable on its right. cout uses the opposite arrow, <<, the stream insertion operator. Read the arrows as the direction the data moves: cin >> age sends data from cin into age, and cout << age sends age out to cout.

If you know Python, age = int(input("Age? ")) does three jobs at once: show a message, read a line, convert it to a number. In C++ you print the message with cout, and cin >> both reads and converts. It converts to whatever type the variable has, so you never write int(...).

Always show a prompt first

A prompt is a message, printed with cout just before a cin, that tells the user what to type. Without one the program sits waiting and the user sees nothing to explain why.

int guests;
cout << "How many guests? ";      // the prompt
cin >> guests;                    // the user types 7, then Enter
cout << "Order " << guests * 2 << " pizzas.\n";

Screen:  How many guests? 7
         Order 14 pizzas.

The keyboard buffer: where typing waits

Keystrokes do not go straight into a variable. They wait in an area of memory called the keyboard buffer (also called the input buffer). The program receives nothing until the user presses Enter. That is why the user can fix a typo with Backspace before the value is read. Enter itself adds one more character to the buffer, the newline, written \n.

One more word you need: whitespace means a space, a tab or a newline.

Each cin >> does three things, in this order:

  1. Skip any whitespace at the front of the buffer.
  2. Take characters as long as they can be part of the variable's type.
  3. Stop at the first character that cannot, and leave it, and everything after it, in the buffer for the next read.

What "can be part of" means depends on the type. An int takes digits, with an optional minus sign in front. A double also takes one decimal point. A char takes exactly one character, which can be a letter, a digit or a symbol.

Reading several values

One statement can read several values by chaining >>. The values fill the variables from left to right.

int a, b;
cout << "Enter two numbers: ";
cin >> a >> b;                   // the user types  15 4  then Enter
cout << a + b;

buffer:         1 5 (space) 4 \n
cin >> a        takes 15, stops at the space      a = 15
buffer:         (space) 4 \n
cin >> b        skips the space, takes 4          b = 4
buffer:         \n
output:         19

The user may separate the values with spaces, tabs or Enter. Typing 15, Enter, 4, Enter gives the same result, because >> skips the whitespace between them.

When a read stops early

A read stops at the first character that does not fit, even in the middle of what the user thinks of as one number. Whatever is left is not lost. The next read takes it without waiting for the user to type anything.

int n;
double d;
cin >> n >> d;          // the user types  12.75  then Enter

buffer:         1 2 . 7 5 \n
cin >> n        int: takes 12, stops at '.'     n = 12
buffer:         . 7 5 \n
cin >> d        double: takes .75               d = 0.75

A char read takes the next character that is not whitespace, even if it is a digit. With the input 7.5 2 z, reading an int, then a double, then a char gives 7, then 0.5, then the character '2'. The z is left in the buffer.

If the user types letters where a number is expected, the read fails. cin then goes into a fail state and ignores every later read until the program resets it. The lesson on characters and strings shows how.

Trap: a comma instead of >>

int x = 0, y = 0;
cin >> x, y;            // the user types  5 8  then Enter
cout << x << " " << y;  // prints 5 0

This compiles, but it reads only x. C++ treats the comma here as "do the left part, then the right part". The left part, cin >> x, reads 5. The right part is just y on its own, which does nothing. So y keeps 0, and the 8 stays unread in the buffer. The correct statement is cin >> x >> y;.

Expressions and the arithmetic operators

An expression is anything that has a value: 7, price, price * 2, pow(2, 3). You can print an expression's value with cout or store it with =.

The operators are +, -, *, / and % (remainder). Remember from the arithmetic lesson: when both sides of / are integers, the fraction is dropped. 7 / 2 is 3 and 6 / 4 is 1, while 7.0 / 2 is 3.5. Python's / always keeps the fraction, so this catches Python users. For positive numbers C++ int division behaves like Python's //.

Precedence: which operator goes first

Precedence is the rank that decides which operator is applied first. Higher rows go first.

RankOperatorsAssociativity
1 (first)( ) groupinginnermost pair first
2unary -, as in -xright to left
3* / %left to right
4+ -left to right
5 (last)= assignmentright to left

A unary operator works on one value. The minus in -x is unary. The minus in a - x is the ordinary subtraction, on rank 4.

Work an expression without parentheses in passes. First do every *, / and %, from left to right. Then do every + and -, from left to right.

20 - 10 / 4 * 3 + 1
pass 1 (* / %):  10 / 4 = 2      (int division)
                 2 * 3 = 6       expression is now 20 - 6 + 1
pass 2 (+ -):    20 - 6 = 14
                 14 + 1 = 15     result 15

Note that % is on the same rank as * and /, not lower. 7 + 5 % 3 * 2 is 7 + (2 * 2), which is 11.

Associativity: ties on the same rank

When two operators of the same rank sit next to each other, associativity decides which goes first. For all the arithmetic operators it is left to right. This matters for -, / and %, where the order changes the answer:

ExpressionC++ doesResultRight to left would give
8 - 3 - 2(8 - 3) - 238 - (3 - 2) = 7
24 / 4 / 2(24 / 4) / 2324 / (4 / 2) = 12
12 / 2 * 3(12 / 2) * 31812 / (2 * 3) = 2
17 % 5 * 3(17 % 5) * 3617 % (5 * 3) = 2

Only unary minus and = go right to left. You will see why that matters for = in the lesson on combined assignment.

Parentheses override everything

Anything inside parentheses is worked out first, the innermost pair before the outer ones. 2 + 3 * 4 is 14, but (2 + 3) * 4 is 20. In ((8 - 2) / (1 + 2)) * 5 the two inner groups give 6 and 3, then 6 / 3 is 2, then 2 * 5 is 10. Extra parentheses never hurt, so add them whenever you are unsure.

Turning algebra into C++

Algebra lets you leave some things out. C++ does not. Two rules cover most cases.

Rule 1: there is no implied multiplication. In algebra 2xy means 2 times x times y. In C++ every multiplication needs a *. Writing 2q or b(c + d) does not compile. The second one looks to C++ like a call to a function named b.

Rule 2: a fraction bar groups. In algebra the bar groups everything above it and everything below it. C++ writes a fraction on one line with /, so you must put that grouping back with parentheses.

AlgebraC++Why
6B6 * Bno implied multiplication
4xy4 * x * ya * between every pair
b(c + d)b * (c + d)b(c + d) looks like a function call
x + y over z(x + y) / zthe whole top is divided
12 over 2k12 / (2 * k)the whole bottom divides
average of a, b, c(a + b + c) / 3the whole sum is divided

See what goes wrong without the parentheses, with k = 2 and a, b, c = 3, 6, 9:

12 / (2 * k)        12 / 4 = 3             correct
12 / 2 * k          (12 / 2) * 2 = 12      divides by 2, then multiplies
(a + b + c) / 3     18 / 3 = 6             correct
a + b + c / 3       3 + 6 + 3 = 12         only c is divided

Powers: pow, not ^

C++ has no exponent operator. Python's ** does not exist, and ^ is not a power: int r = 2 ^ 3; compiles but stores 1, because ^ is a different operation on bits. For powers, use the pow function from <cmath>.

double area = pow(side, 2.0);   // side squared

This is a function call. The values in the parentheses, side and 2.0, are the arguments: the data sent into the function. pow raises its first argument to the power of its second and sends back the answer, its return value, which is stored in area. pow returns a double, even when both arguments are ints.

  • pow(2, 5) is 2 * 2 * 2 * 2 * 2 = 32. It returns 32.0, but cout drops trailing zeros and prints 32.
  • pow(9, 0.5) is 9 to the power one half, which is the square root of 9. It prints 3.
  • The area of a circle, πr², becomes 3.14159 * pow(r, 2). With r = 2 that prints 12.5664.

Mistakes students make

  • Writing the arrows the wrong way: cin << x or cout >> x.
  • Reading with no prompt, so the user does not know the program is waiting.
  • Writing cin >> a, b; and expecting b to be read.
  • Thinking a read always takes everything up to Enter. 3.9 read into an int gives 3 and leaves .9 for the next read.
  • Working strictly left to right and ignoring precedence: 2 + 3 * 4 is 14, not 20.
  • Working same-rank operators right to left: 8 - 3 - 2 is 3, not 7.
  • Forgetting integer division: 6 / 4 is 1.
  • Writing 2q or b(c + d) without a *.
  • Leaving out the parentheses around a numerator or a denominator.
  • Writing 2 ^ 3 for a power.

What to remember for the test

  • cin >> var; reads. The arrows point the way the data moves. >> is extraction, << is insertion.
  • Print a prompt before every read.
  • Typed characters wait in the keyboard buffer until Enter is pressed.
  • >> skips leading whitespace, takes only characters that fit the type, and leaves the rest in the buffer.
  • Read several values with cin >> a >> b;, never with a comma.
  • Precedence: parentheses, then unary minus, then * / %, then + -, then =.
  • Associativity breaks ties on one rank: left to right for arithmetic, right to left for unary minus and =.
  • No implied multiplication. Put parentheses around a numerator or denominator with more than one term.
  • pow(base, exponent) returns a double. The values passed in are arguments, the value sent back is the return value.

lessons.title: Type conversion, overflow and casting
lessons.html:
The idea: both sides of an operator must have the same type

Every value in C++ has a data type. The computer does arithmetic on two values of the same type: two ints, or two doubles. So when an operator gets two different types, as in 5 + 2.5, C++ first converts one of them so they match. It does this on its own, without being asked. The textbook calls this automatic conversion type coercion.

Hold on to one fact: the conversion happens one operator at a time, at the moment that operator runs. An operator looks only at its own two operands. It does not look ahead to the rest of the statement or to the variable that will receive the answer. Almost every trap in this lesson comes from that.

The ranking of types

To decide which way to convert, C++ ranks the numeric types. A higher type can hold a wider range of values, or fractions, so converting up is normally safe.

long double           highest
double
float
unsigned long long
long long
unsigned long
long
unsigned int
int                   lowest

char, short and unsigned short are not on the list, because they never take part in arithmetic as themselves (Rule 1 below).

Converting a value to a higher type is promotion. Converting it to a lower type is demotion, also called narrowing. Demotion can lose data: the fraction of a double, or part of a number too big for the smaller type. Storing a long value in an int is a demotion.

The three rules of automatic conversion

Rule 1: char, short and unsigned short are promoted to int whenever they are used in arithmetic.

cout << 'A' + 1;

'A'        a char, stored as its code: 65 in ASCII
'A' + 1    the char is promoted to int: 65 + 1 = 66
           the result is an int, so cout prints 66

The result is an int, not a char, so it prints as 66, not B. To get the letter you convert it back: static_cast<char>('A' + 1) prints B (casts are explained below). Storing it in a char variable also works: after char c = 'A' + 2;, c holds 'C'.

Rule 2: when an operator's two operands have different types, the lower-ranked one is promoted to the higher-ranked type. The result has that higher type.

5 + 2.5    int and double: 5 becomes 5.0
           5.0 + 2.5 = 7.5, a double
5 / 2      int and int: nothing to convert
           integer division: 2
5 / 2.0    int and double: 5 becomes 5.0
           5.0 / 2.0 = 2.5

One double operand is enough to make a division keep its fraction. The variable itself is not changed by a promotion. Only the copy used in the arithmetic is converted.

Rule 3: a value stored in a variable with = is converted to that variable's type. This happens last, after the right side has been fully worked out.

int n = 7.9;       7.9 converted to int:          n = 7
double d = 4 / 3;  right side first: int / int = 1
                   then 1 converted to double:    d = 1.0
cout << n << " " << d;                // prints 7 1

Two lessons there. First, converting a double to an int truncates: it chops off the fraction and never rounds. 7.9 becomes 7, 8.9 becomes 8, and -7.9 becomes -7. Second, a double on the left of = does not rescue an integer division on the right. By the time the value reaches d, the fraction is already gone. (cout prints 1.0 as 1.)

All three rules in one statement

int qty = 4;
float price = 1.5f;     // the f makes 1.5 a float
double total;
total = price * qty;

step 1  price * qty is float * int (Rule 2)
        qty is promoted to float: 4.0f
        1.5f * 4.0f = 6.0f, a float
step 2  the float 6.0 is assigned to a double (Rule 3)
        it is converted to double as it is stored

Notice what does not happen: the multiplication is not done in double just because total is a double. The * only knows about a float and an int.

Overflow and underflow

Each integer type has a fixed size, so it has a smallest and a largest value. On most systems a short is 2 bytes and holds -32,768 to 32,767. An unsigned short (unsigned means no minus sign is allowed) holds 0 to 65,535.

  • Overflow: a variable is given a value larger than its type's maximum, such as 40,000 in a short.
  • Underflow: a variable is given a value smaller than its type's minimum. For floating-point types, underflow also means a value too close to zero to be stored, such as 10 to the power -400 in a double.

What happens to an integer? It usually wraps around, like a car odometer rolling over from 99999 to 00000. One step past the largest value lands on the smallest. One step below the smallest lands on the largest.

short s = 32767;            // the maximum
s = s + 1;
cout << s;                  // typically prints -32768

unsigned short u = 65535;   // the maximum
u = u + 1;
cout << u;                  // prints 0

unsigned short z = 0;       // the minimum
z = z - 1;
cout << z;                  // prints 65535

To work out a wrap by hand, count the steps past the end. For an unsigned short, one step past 65,535 is 0, two steps is 1, and so on. For a short, one step below -32,768 is 32,767, two steps is 32,766.

The fact examiners test most: no error and no warning appears when this happens. The program keeps running with a wrong number. Prevent it by choosing a type big enough for the values, for example int or long long instead of short.

How certain is the wrap? For unsigned types C++ guarantees it. For signed types such as short and int it does not. Wrap-around is what typical systems do with a short, and it is the answer the textbook expects, but a program must never rely on it.

For floating-point types the result depends on the system: the program may carry on with a wrong value, stop with an error, or, on underflow, store 0. On a typical PC today a double that overflows becomes inf (infinity) and one that underflows becomes 0.

Type casting: converting on purpose

Sometimes you need a conversion that C++ would not do by itself. A type cast expression forces it:

static_cast<DataType>(Value)

The type you want goes inside the angle brackets. The value to convert goes inside the parentheses. static_cast<double>(total) means "the value of total, as a double".

A cast makes a converted copy. It never changes the variable.

double t = 3.75;
int whole = static_cast<int>(t);   // a truncated copy of t: 3
cout << whole << " " << t;         // prints 3 3.75

t still holds 3.75. Like any conversion to int, the cast truncates: static_cast<int>(2.99) is 2.

The main use: avoiding integer division

To average ints, cast one operand before the division, so that Rule 2 makes the division keep its fraction. Where the cast goes decides everything:

int sum = 9, count = 4;

sum / count                         9 / 4       = 2
static_cast<double>(sum) / count    9.0 / 4     = 2.25
sum / static_cast<double>(count)    9 / 4.0     = 2.25
static_cast<double>(sum / count)    (9 / 4) = 2, then 2.0

The last line is the classic bug. The parentheses after static_cast<double> hold sum / count, so that integer division runs first and gives 2. The cast then turns 2 into 2.0. It is too late to bring back the .25. The line compiles, but the cast does nothing useful.

Casting with char, and older cast styles

A char is stored as its character code, so casting between char and int changes how the value is shown: static_cast<int>('A') is 65 and static_cast<char>(66) prints B.

You may see older cast styles: (double)sum, from the C language, and double(sum). They do the same job, but static_cast is the form the textbook uses.

Mistakes students make

  • Expecting int n = 7.9; to round to 8. It truncates to 7.
  • Expecting double d = 4 / 3; to hold 1.33333. The int division happens first, so d is 1.
  • Putting the whole division inside the cast: static_cast<double>(sum / count).
  • Thinking 'A' + 1 is a char. It is the int 66.
  • Thinking the receiving variable decides the type of the arithmetic.
  • Thinking a cast changes the variable it reads.
  • Thinking integer overflow stops the program with an error.
  • Mixing up the words. Overflow is above the maximum, underflow below the minimum (or too close to zero, for floating point). Promotion goes up the ranking, demotion goes down.
  • Writing the cast in the wrong shape, such as static_cast(double)<total>.

What to remember for the test

  • Type coercion is the automatic conversion C++ does when operand types differ.
  • Rule 1: char and short become int in arithmetic. Rule 2: the lower-ranked operand is promoted to the higher type. Rule 3: an assigned value is converted to the variable's type.
  • Conversions happen one operator at a time. The variable on the left does not change the arithmetic on the right.
  • double to int truncates. It never rounds.
  • Integer overflow and underflow give no error. Integers typically wrap around, and unsigned types always do.
  • Floating-point overflow and underflow depend on the system.
  • static_cast<Type>(value) returns a converted copy. Cast an operand, not the finished division.

lessons.title: Combined assignment and hand tracing
lessons.book: Sections 3.6 and 3.10, pages 108 to 112 and 133 to 135
lessons.html:
The idea: a variable updated from its own value

Programs constantly change a variable based on what it already holds: add a price to a running total, subtract a withdrawal from a balance, double a quantity. The key to reading these statements is how = works. The right side is worked out first, using the values the variables hold right now. Only then is the result stored in the variable on the left, replacing what was there.

int balance = 100;
balance = balance - 20;

right side first:  balance - 20  is  100 - 20 = 80
then store:        balance = 80     (the 100 is gone)

In algebra balance = balance - 20 would be impossible. In C++ it is an instruction, not an equation: "take the current balance, subtract 20, put the answer back in balance".

Assignment has a value, and it goes right to left

An assignment does two things. It stores a value, and the whole assignment expression has that value, so it can be used inside a bigger statement. Assignment also associates right to left: when several = appear in a row, the rightmost one happens first.

int a, b;
a = b = 4;        // means  a = (b = 4)

step 1   b = 4     b holds 4, and this part has the value 4
step 2   a = 4     a holds 4

So p = q = r = 6; gives all three variables the value 6. Python allows a = b = 4 too, with the same result.

Combined assignment operators

Because "update a variable from its own value" is so common, C++ has a shorthand. The combined assignment operators (the textbook also calls them compound or arithmetic assignment operators) put an arithmetic operator right in front of =:

OperatorExampleMeansIf x was 10, x becomes
+=x += 5;x = x + 5;15
-=x -= 5;x = x - 5;5
*=x *= 5;x = x * 5;50
/=x /= 5;x = x / 5;2
%=x %= 5;x = x % 5;0

Python has the same operators, except that Python's /= always keeps the fraction. A chain of them is traced one line at a time, each line starting from the value the previous line left:

int x = 7;
x += 5;     // 7 + 5  = 12
x *= 3;     // 12 * 3 = 36
x -= 6;     // 36 - 6 = 30
x /= 4;     // 30 / 4 = 7    (int division drops .5)
x %= 4;     // 7 % 4  = 3    (the remainder)
cout << x;  // prints 3

Rule: the whole right side goes first

Combined assignment has the same very low precedence as =. Everything on its right is worked out first, as if it were in parentheses, and only then combined with the variable.

int x = 5, a = 2, b = 3;
x *= a + b;        // means  x = x * (a + b)
                   // a + b is 5, then 5 * 5 = 25
                   // NOT x * a + b, which would be 13

The same goes for -=: with x = 10 and y = 4, x -= y - 1; means x = x - (y - 1), which is 10 - 3 = 7, not 10 - 4 - 1 = 5.

Rule: the variable's type decides the arithmetic

x /= 2 is x = x / 2, so the usual division rules apply. If x is an int, it is integer division.

int i = 7;
i /= 2;        // 7 / 2 is int division: i is 3
double d = 7;
d /= 2;        // 7.0 / 2 = 3.5: d is 3.5

%= needs ints, just like %. d %= 2 with a double does not compile.

The variable must already hold a value. int total; total += 5; uses total before it has been given a value. Its starting value is unpredictable (programmers call it garbage), so the result is unpredictable too. Start running totals at 0: int total = 0;.

Trap: =+ is not +=

The arithmetic sign comes first, then =, with no space. Swap them and you get something else:

int count = 10;
count =+ 3;     // read as  count = +3;   count is 3, not 13
count =- 3;     // read as  count = -3;   count is -3
count =* 3;     // does not compile

=+ compiles because +3 is a legal way to write positive 3, so the statement quietly becomes a plain assignment. That is what makes it dangerous. + = with a space does not compile either.

Hand tracing

Hand tracing means playing the computer on paper. You step through the code one statement at a time and record each variable's value after every statement. It finds logic errors: mistakes that compile and run but give a wrong answer, such as a wrong operator or a missing pair of parentheses. The compiler cannot catch those. Hand tracing is also exactly how you answer "what does this print" questions on the test.

The method:

  1. Make a column for each variable, and one for the output.
  2. Write one row per statement, in the order the program runs them.
  3. In each row, write the new value of the variable that changes. Copy the others down unchanged.
  4. Write ? for a variable that has no value yet.
  5. When a statement uses a variable, take the value from the latest row, not from the start.
int x = 2, y = 5, z;
z = x + y;
x = z * 2;
y = x - z;
z = y % 4;
cout << x << " " << y << " " << z;
StatementxyzOutput
int x = 2, y = 5, z;25?
z = x + y;257
x = z * 2;1457
y = x - z;1477
z = y % 4;1473
cout147314 7 3

Look at the row for y = x - z. It uses x = 14, the value from the row above, not the starting 2. Using a stale value is the number one tracing mistake.

A second trace, with a chained assignment and combined operators:

StatementmnNote
m = n = 8;88right to left: n first, then m
m /= 3;288 / 3 is 2, int division
n -= m * 2;24n = 8 - (2 * 2)
m += n;642 + 4

Using a trace to find a logic error

This program is supposed to average three test scores:

double s1 = 70, s2 = 80, s3 = 90;
double avg = s1 + s2 + s3 / 3;
cout << avg;

It compiles and runs. Trace it: / goes before +, so s3 / 3 is 30, and then 70 + 80 + 30 is 180. Now compare with a hand-worked answer: the average of 70, 80 and 90 is 80. Better still, an average can never be larger than the largest value, so 180 is clearly wrong. The trace points straight at the missing parentheses. The fix, (s1 + s2 + s3) / 3, gives 240 / 3 = 80.

Mistakes students make

  • Using a variable's starting value after a statement has already changed it.
  • Reading x *= a + b as x * a + b. The whole right side goes first.
  • Writing =+ instead of +=, and getting a plain assignment.
  • Forgetting that /= on an int is integer division.
  • Thinking a = b = 4 runs left to right. The rightmost = happens first.
  • Using += on a variable that was never given a starting value.
  • Forgetting the parentheses in an average, so only the last value is divided.

What to remember for the test

  • In an assignment the right side is worked out first, with the current values, then stored.
  • Assignment goes right to left: a = b = 4 sets b, then a.
  • x op= y means x = x op (y), with the whole right side in parentheses.
  • The variable's type decides the arithmetic: int i = 9; i /= 2; leaves 4.
  • =+ is a plain assignment of a positive number. The operator is +=.
  • Hand tracing: a column per variable, a row per statement, always use the latest value. It finds logic errors the compiler cannot.

lessons.title: Formatting output
lessons.html:
The idea: cout has settings you can change

By default cout prints a number in its shortest natural form, with no extra spaces. That is fine for one value, but not for a receipt where the prices must line up, or for money that must show exactly two decimals. To control the look, you send cout a stream manipulator: something you put in a cout chain with << that prints nothing itself but changes how the values after it are printed.

Think of cout as having a few dials. Most manipulators turn a dial and leave it there, so the setting is sticky: it stays in effect until you change it. One manipulator, setw, is one-shot: it applies to the next value only. Keep those two kinds apart and most of this lesson follows.

Manipulators that take a number in parentheses, setw(n) and setprecision(n), need #include <iomanip> (input/output manipulators). Leaving it out is a compile error. The ones without parentheses, fixed, showpoint, left and right, come with <iostream>.

If you know Python, f"{x:8.2f}" is close to setw(8) << fixed << setprecision(2) << x. The difference is that in C++ most of those settings stay on for later values.

setw: the field width

A field is a block of character positions set aside for one value. setw(n) makes the next value take up at least n positions. By default the value is right-justified: it sits at the right end of the field and spaces fill the left.

cout << "[" << setw(6) << 42 << "]";

field of 6:   _ _ _ _ 4 2     42 needs 2, so 6 - 2 = 4 spaces
prints:       [    42]

The counting rule: spaces added = width minus the number of characters in the value. Every character counts, including a minus sign, a decimal point, and letters or spaces in a string.

setw(7) << -3.5     "-3.5" is 4 characters: 3 spaces   [   -3.5]
setw(6) << "Bob"    "Bob" is 3 characters: 3 spaces    [   Bob]
setw(3) << 98765    5 characters, wider than 3:
                    nothing is cut, the field grows   [98765]

setw never cuts a value short. If the value is wider than the field, it is printed in full with no padding.

setw is one-shot. It applies to the next value printed and then turns itself off:

cout << "[" << setw(4) << 1 << 2 << "]";

setw(4) << 1    field of 4: 3 spaces + 1
<< 2            no width now: printed right after
prints:         [   12]

To give every value its own field, write setw again before each one.

left and right

left puts the value at the left edge of the field, with the spaces after it. right, the default, puts the spaces before it. Both are sticky: after left, every later field is left-justified until right is used.

cout << left  << "[" << setw(6) << "ab" << "]";   // [ab    ]
cout << right << "[" << setw(6) << "ab" << "]";   // [    ab]

They only matter when setw makes a field wider than the value. A common layout is a label in a left-justified field, then a number in a right-justified field, as in the receipt below.

setprecision without fixed: significant digits

Normally cout shows a floating-point number with at most 6 significant digits and drops any trailing zeros. That is why 5.0 prints as 5.

Significant digits are counted from the first non-zero digit, on both sides of the decimal point together. 123.456 has six: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. In 0.0123456 the leading zeros do not count, so it also starts at the 1.

setprecision(n) changes the maximum to n significant digits. The last digit kept is rounded.

Valuesetprecision(2)setprecision(4)
3.141593.13.142
123.4561.2e+02123.5
0.01234560.0120.01235
2.52.52.5

Three things to notice in that table.

  • It is a maximum, not a target. 2.5 needs only 2 digits, so it prints as 2.5 even with precision 4. No zeros are added. In the same way setprecision(5) << 80.0 prints 80.
  • Rounding: 3.14159 to 4 digits looks at the fifth digit, 5, and rounds up to 3.142.
  • Too few digits for the whole part: 123.456 has three digits before the point, but precision 2 allows only two. cout cannot write it in ordinary form, so it switches to scientific (E) notation, which you met in the floating-point lesson. 1.2e+02 means 1.2 times 10 to the 2nd, about 120. In the same way setprecision(3) << 45678.9 prints 4.57e+04.

fixed: digits after the decimal point

fixed switches to fixed-point notation: ordinary digits with a decimal point, never E notation. It also changes what precision means. With fixed, setprecision(n) means exactly n digits after the decimal point, rounded, with zeros added if needed.

cout << fixed << setprecision(2);
cout << 3.14159;   // 3.14       rounded to 2 decimals
cout << 2.5;       // 2.50       a zero is added
cout << 123.456;   // 123.46     digits before the point don't count
cout << 45678.9;   // 45678.90   no E notation with fixed
cout << 7;         // 7          an int is not affected

Precision, fixed and showpoint only affect floating-point values. An int always prints as a plain whole number.

The standard way to print money is one line near the top of the program, cout << fixed << setprecision(2);. Because both settings are sticky, every amount after it shows two decimals.

showpoint: keep the trailing zeros

Without fixed, showpoint forces the decimal point and trailing zeros to appear, so that every significant digit allowed by the precision is shown. Precision still counts significant digits, on both sides of the point.

cout << showpoint << 5.0;          // 5.00000  (default: 6 digits)
cout << setprecision(3) << 1.5;    // 1.50     (3 digits: 1, 5, 0)
cout << 20.0;                      // 20.0     (3 digits: 2, 0, 0)

Compare fixed, which would print 1.500 and 20.000 with precision 3, because it counts only digits after the point. Together with fixed, showpoint makes no difference in normal use, since fixed already shows the decimals.

Which settings stay

ManipulatorNeedsLasts
setw(n)<iomanip>next value only
setprecision(n)<iomanip>until changed
fixed<iostream>until changed
showpoint<iostream>until changed
left, right<iostream>until changed

Putting it together: a receipt

cout << fixed << setprecision(2);
cout << left << setw(8) << "Tea"
     << right << setw(7) << 2.5 << "\n";
cout << left << setw(8) << "Muffin"
     << right << setw(7) << 12.0 << "\n";

Output:
Tea        2.50
Muffin    12.00

Count the first line. "Tea" is 3 characters in a field of 8, left-justified, so 5 spaces follow it. 2.5 becomes 2.50, 4 characters in a field of 7, right-justified, so 3 spaces come before it. That is 8 spaces between "Tea" and "2.50". The second line has 2 + 2 = 4 spaces, so the decimal points line up.

Order inside a chain: setw(10) << fixed << setprecision(2) << total still gives total a 10-wide field. Manipulators are not printed values, so they do not use up the width.

Mistakes students make

  • Expecting setw to apply to the values after the next one.
  • Miscounting spaces by forgetting that the decimal point and minus sign take a position.
  • Expecting setw to cut off a value that is too wide.
  • Forgetting that without fixed, setprecision counts significant digits, not decimal places.
  • Expecting setprecision alone to add zeros. Only fixed or showpoint add them.
  • Thinking precision changes how an int prints.
  • Thinking fixed with setprecision(3) means 3 significant digits. It means 3 decimal places.
  • Forgetting #include <iomanip>.

What to remember for the test

  • setw(n): next value only, right-justified by default, spaces = width minus characters, never cuts.
  • left and right are sticky.
  • No fixed: precision = maximum significant digits (default 6), trailing zeros dropped, E notation if the whole part does not fit.
  • With fixed: precision = exact digits after the point, zeros added.
  • showpoint without fixed: shows all the significant digits, with trailing zeros.
  • setprecision, fixed, showpoint, left, right stay until changed. Ints are never affected by precision.
  • setw and setprecision need <iomanip>.

lessons.title: Characters and strings with cin
lessons.html:
The one idea behind this whole lesson: the input buffer

Your keystrokes do not go straight into a variable. They wait in a line called the input buffer (the book also calls it the keyboard buffer). Nothing reaches your program until you press Enter, and Enter is itself a character that joins the line. It is the newline character, written '\n' in C++.

Suppose the user types 30, presses Enter, types Bob and presses Enter. The buffer now holds seven characters, in this order:

3  0  \n  B  o  b  \n

Every input statement takes characters from the front of that line. Whatever it does not take stays there and is the first thing the next input statement sees. One more word you need: whitespace means a space, a tab or a newline.

If you know Python, this is the big difference from input(), which always takes one whole line. In C++ each read starts exactly where the last one stopped, even in the middle of a line.

The input tools differ in only three ways: what they skip first, where they stop, and what they leave behind.

ToolSkips leading whitespace?StopsLeaves in the buffer
cin >> x;YesAt the first character that cannot be part of the value. For a string that is the next whitespace. For a number it is usually whitespace, but any character that does not fit also stops it, such as the '.' when 3.9 is read into an int.That character and everything after it. The newline from Enter stays.
getline(cin, s);NoAt the first newline.Whatever comes after that newline. The newline itself is removed, and it is not stored in s.
cin.get(ch);NoAfter exactly one character, whatever it is.Everything after that one character.
cin.ignore();NoAfter throwing away exactly one character.Everything after that one character.
cin.ignore(n, '\n');NoAfter throwing away n characters, or as soon as it has thrown away a newline, whichever comes first.Everything after that point.

cin >> reads one word

With a string variable, cin >> skips any whitespace at the front, then takes characters until it meets whitespace again. So it reads one word, never a whole line.

string name;
cin >> name;          // the user types Mary Ann and presses Enter
buffer before:   M a r y (space) A n n \n
cin >> name      takes Mary, stops at the space
name is now:     Mary
buffer after:    (space) A n n \n      still waiting

Ann is not lost. It is still in the buffer, and the next cin >> would read it without waiting for the user to type anything.

getline reads a whole line

To read text that contains spaces, use getline(cin, name);. It takes two things inside the parentheses: where to read from (cin) and the string variable to fill. It reads every character up to the newline, spaces included, then removes the newline from the buffer and throws it away.

string name;
getline(cin, name);   // the user types Mary Ann and presses Enter
buffer before:   M a r y (space) A n n \n
getline          takes everything up to \n, then removes the \n
name is now:     Mary Ann
buffer after:    (empty)

getline only fills a string. You cannot use it to read into an int or a char, and you cannot write it with >>.

The classic bug: cin >> and then getline

int age;
string name;
cin >> age;           // the user types 30 and presses Enter
getline(cin, name);   // meant to read Bob

Trace it with the buffer:

buffer:          3 0 \n
cin >> age       takes 30, stops at \n and leaves it
buffer:          \n
getline          does not skip whitespace. It sees \n at once,
                 so the "line" it reads is empty
name is now:     ""  (an empty string)

getline found a newline already waiting, so it finished immediately. The name is empty because there were zero characters in front of that newline. The program does not even pause for the user to type the name. If Bob is typed later it just sits in the buffer.

The fix is to throw the leftover newline away before calling getline:

cin >> age;           // buffer after:  \n
cin.ignore();         // discards one character, the \n.  buffer: (empty)
getline(cin, name);   // buffer is empty, so the program waits.
                      // The user types Bob.
                      // name is now Bob

cin.ignore(); removes one character. That is enough only if the newline is the very next character. If the user typed 30 years, one ignore() removes just the space, and getline then reads years. The stronger form handles that:

cin.ignore(100, '\n');   // discard up to 100 characters,
                         // but stop as soon as a newline has been discarded

In short: it skips the rest of the current line, newline included.

When do you need it? Only when a cin >> is followed by getline or cin.get. You do not need it between two cin >> statements, because >> skips leading whitespace by itself. You do not need it between two getline calls either, because each getline removes its own newline.

cin.get reads exactly one character

cin >> ch; with a char skips whitespace and reads the next visible character. cin.get(ch); skips nothing: it reads the very next character, even if that is a space or a newline.

char a, b;             // the user types  x y  and presses Enter
                       // buffer:  x (space) y \n
cin.get(a);            // a is 'x'
cin.get(b);            // b is the space, not 'y'

With cin >> a >> b; the space would be skipped and b would be 'y'.

  • It has three forms. cin.get(ch); and ch = cin.get(); both put the next character in ch. cin.get(); with nothing in the parentheses reads one character and throws it away. Programs use that last form to pause until the user presses Enter.
  • It hits the same trap as getline: after cin >> number; the next cin.get(ch) reads the leftover '\n' instead of waiting. Put cin.ignore(); between them.
  • Why the dot? get and ignore are member functions of cin: functions that belong to the cin object, so you call them as cin.get(...) and cin.ignore(...). getline is called differently: cin goes inside the parentheses.

Things you can do with a string

string first = "Ada", last = "Lovelace";
cout << first.length();          // 3   the number of characters
cout << first[0];                // A   positions start at 0
                                 //     (first[2] is the last a)
string full = first + " " + last; // Ada Lovelace
                                  // + joins strings (concatenation)
first += "!";                     // += adds to the end of first: Ada!

A space counts as a character, so full.length() is 3 + 1 + 8 = 12. length is a member function of the string, so it needs the dot and the parentheses: full.length().

Character functions from <cctype>

Add #include <cctype> to use them. Each one takes a single character.

  • isdigit(c) is true when c is one of '0' to '9'. isalpha(c) is true when it is a letter.
  • toupper(c) and tolower(c) return the capital or small version of a letter, and return any other character unchanged. They do not change c itself.
  • Trap: toupper returns an int (the character's numeric code), not a char. cout << toupper('q'); prints 81. Store the result in a char first and it prints as a letter: char c = toupper('q'); cout << c; prints Q.

When the input is the wrong type

If the program runs cin >> n; for an int and the user types abc, the letters cannot be turned into a number. cin goes into a fail state: that read fails, the letters stay in the buffer, and every later read from cin does nothing until the program clears the error. This is why a program can seem to skip all the rest of its input after one bad entry. To recover, a program calls cin.clear(); to reset the error and then cin.ignore(100, '\n'); to throw away the bad line.

Mistakes students make

  • Using cin >> name for a full name and getting only the first word.
  • Calling getline straight after cin >> and getting an empty string.
  • Thinking cin.ignore() empties the whole buffer. With no arguments it removes one character.
  • Writing cin.getline(name) or getline >> name. The form for a string is getline(cin, name);.
  • Putting cin.ignore() where no newline is waiting, for example before the first input. It then throws away the first character the user wanted to enter.
  • Expecting first + last to change first. + makes a new string. Only = or += changes a variable.
  • Counting from 1: the first character of s is s[0].
  • Printing toupper(c) directly and getting a number.

What to remember for the test

  • cin >>: skips whitespace, reads one word or one value, leaves the newline.
  • getline(cin, s): skips nothing, reads the whole line, removes the newline.
  • cin.get(ch): reads one character of any kind, including a space or newline.
  • cin.ignore() discards one character. cin.ignore(n, '\n') discards the rest of the line.
  • A cin >> followed by getline or cin.get needs a cin.ignore() in between.
  • For any "what does this print" input question, write out the buffer and cross characters off as each statement takes them.

lessons.title: Math library, random numbers and problem solving
lessons.book: Sections 3.9 and 3.11, pages 128 to 133 and 135 to 140
lessons.html:
The idea: ready-made functions you call by name

C++ comes with ready-made code for common calculations: square roots, powers, rounding, logarithms. Each one is a function, a named piece of code that does one job. To call it, write its name and put the values it needs in parentheses. Those values are the arguments. The value the function sends back is its return value, and the program uses it right where the call was written.

The math functions are declared in the header <cmath>, so a program that uses them starts with #include <cmath>. If you know Python, this is like import math, except that you call sqrt(x) directly, not math.sqrt(x).

Here is one call, traced step by step. The formula is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs a and b, √(a² + b²):

double a = 3, b = 4;
double c = sqrt(a * a + b * b);

1. Work out the argument:  a * a + b * b  is  9 + 16 = 25
2. Call the function:      sqrt(25.0) returns 5.0
3. Use the return value:   c is now 5.0

The argument is always worked out before the function runs. Hold on to that: the biggest trap in this lesson comes from it. Notice also that the formula takes one square root of the whole sum. Wrong versions an examiner will offer, with a = 3 and b = 4:

  • sqrt(a) + sqrt(b) takes roots of the legs: 1.73205 + 2 = 3.73205.
  • sqrt(a * a) + sqrt(b * b) is just 3 + 4 = 7. The square root of a sum is not the sum of the square roots.
  • pow(a * a + b * b, 1 / 2) gives 1. The pow section below shows why.

Almost all the math functions take and return double. If you pass an int, it is converted to a double first, and the result is a double even when it is a whole number. cout drops trailing zeros, so sqrt(81) returns 9.0 and prints as 9. One exception: abs given an int returns an int, so abs(-7) is the int 7.

The functions to know

CallWhat it givesExampleResult
sqrt(x)square rootsqrt(81)9
pow(x, y)x to the power ypow(2, 5)32
abs(x)absolute value: the number without its minus signabs(-7)7
ceil(x)rounds up to a whole numberceil(2.1)3
floor(x)rounds down to a whole numberfloor(2.9)2
round(x)nearest whole numberround(2.4)2
fmod(x, y)remainder of x divided by y, for doublesfmod(10.0, 3)1
exp(x)e to the power xexp(1.0)2.71828
log(x)natural logarithm, base elog(100.0)4.60517
log10(x)logarithm, base 10log10(100.0)2

Rounding: ceil, floor and round

Picture a number line. ceil (short for ceiling) moves to the nearest whole number on the right, the larger side. floor moves to the nearest whole number on the left, the smaller side. round moves to whichever whole number is closer, and a value exactly halfway goes away from zero. A value that is already whole stays the same in all three.

Compare them on the same numbers. The last column is what a cast to int does (you met static_cast in the lesson on type conversion): it just chops off the fraction.

xfloor(x)ceil(x)round(x)static_cast<int>(x)
2.12322
2.52332
-2.1-3-2-2-2
-2.5-3-2-3-2

Two things to notice. With negative numbers "up" still means toward the larger number, so ceil(-2.1) is -2 and floor(-2.1) is -3. And halves go away from zero on both sides, so round(-2.5) is -3, not -2.

Use ceil when you must buy whole units and cannot fall short: 2.1 gallons of paint means buying 3. The result is a double, but you can store it in an int: int cans = ceil(2.1); stores 3.

fmod: the remainder for doubles

The % operator only works on integers. 7.5 % 2 does not compile. For doubles use fmod(x, y). It answers this question: after taking out as many whole copies of y as fit into x, what is left?

fmod(7.5, 2)    2 fits into 7.5 three whole times
                3 * 2 = 6
                7.5 - 6 = 1.5          result 1.5
fmod(10.0, 3)   3 fits 3 times, 10 - 9 = 1      result 1

pow, roots and the integer-division trap

pow(base, exponent) raises the base to the exponent: pow(2, 5) is 2 * 2 * 2 * 2 * 2 = 32. Roots are fractional powers. A square root is the power one half, so pow(16, 0.5) is 4, the same as sqrt(16). A cube root is the power one third: pow(8.0, 1.0 / 3) is 2, because 2 * 2 * 2 = 8.

Now the trap. The argument is worked out before pow runs, so 1 / 3 is calculated first. Both numbers are ints, so it is integer division, which drops the fraction:

pow(8.0, 1 / 3)
1. argument: 1 / 3 is int / int, the fraction is dropped: 0
2. pow(8.0, 0) returns 1 (any number to the power 0 is 1)
result: 1, not 2

pow(8.0, 1.0 / 3)
1. argument: 1.0 / 3 is 0.333..., a double
2. pow(8.0, 0.333...) returns 2
result: 2

The same thing happens with pow(x, 1 / 2), which is always 1. Write 1.0 / 2 or 0.5, or use sqrt. The rule from the arithmetic lesson still holds inside parentheses: int divided by int gives an int.

exp and the two logarithms

The number e is about 2.71828. exp(x) gives e to the power x, so exp(0.0) is 1 (any number to the power 0 is 1) and exp(1.0) is 2.71828.

A logarithm asks the reverse question: which power do I need? log10(x) asks "10 to what power gives x?" and log(x) asks "e to what power gives x?". So log is the natural logarithm, not base 10. Python's math.log(x) is the same.

log10(100.0)    10 to the power 2 is 100       prints 2
